hero.subtitle: The original request/response protocol that launched the World Wide Web

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP/1.0 is the first widely-deployed version of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol. It defines the basic request/response model that underlies all communication on the World Wide Web.

HTTP was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989 as part of his proposal for a distributed hypertext system. HTTP/1.0 was the first version to be formally documented, codifying practices already in widespread use.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
HTTP is a stateless, request/response protocol. A client sends a request message to a server, and the server returns a response message.

Stateless
Each request is independent. The server retains no memory of previous requests from the same client. State management (sessions, cookies) must be built on top.
Text-Based
HTTP/1.0 messages are human-readable text. Request and response headers are ASCII text lines terminated by CRLF.
One Request Per Connection
In HTTP/1.0, each request opens a new TCP connection, sends the request, receives the response, and closes the connection. This is simple but inefficient.

sections.title: Request
sections.content:
An HTTP request consists of a request line, headers, and an optional body:

HTTP/1.0 Request Format
GET /index.html HTTP/1.0
Host: www.example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0
Accept: text/html
MethodThe action to perform (GET, POST, HEAD)Token
Request-URIThe resource being requestedURI
HTTP-VersionAlways "HTTP/1.0"String

sections.title: Response
sections.content:
An HTTP response consists of a status line, headers, and an optional body:

HTTP/1.0 Response Format
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 1234

<html>...</html>

sections.title: Methods
sections.content:
HTTP/1.0 defines three methods:

GETRetrieve a resource. The most common method. Must be safe and idempotent.
HEADSame as GET but returns only headers, not the body. Used for checking if a resource exists.
POSTSubmit data to be processed (e.g., form submission). May create or modify resources.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers grouped by category:

1xxInformational — Request received, continuing process
2xxSuccess — Request received, understood, and accepted
3xxRedirection — Further action needed to complete request
4xxClient Error — Request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled
5xxServer Error — Server failed to fulfill a valid request
200 OKThe request has succeeded
301 Moved PermanentlyResource has been permanently moved
304 Not ModifiedResource has not changed since last request
400 Bad RequestServer cannot process the request due to client error
404 Not FoundThe requested resource could not be found
500 Internal Server ErrorUnexpected server-side error
